land.text: Costa Rica, which in 1838 'formally withdrew and proclaimed itself sovereign' (infobox: from the Federal Republic of Central America, 14 November 1838); it already held the Nicoya Partido from the town-hall vote of 25 July 1824 (Santa Cruz followed three days later; the town of Guanacaste alone declined, and the page later speaks of 'the acquisition of Guanacaste, in the north')

predecessors.note: The Costa Rica page also says Costa Rica 'formally declared independence in 1847'; the 1838 date is the infobox's. Costa Rica had seceded earlier in 1829-1831 (carried by the federation's dossier).

capitals.name: San José
capitals.note: After the 1823 Battle of Ochomogo 'Cartago lost its capital status to San José' (Costa Rica page), so San José was the capital throughout the republic's life.

correction.text: the 1840 shape (present Costa Rica including the Nicoya Partido incorporated in 1824) held for 1838-1839: Costa Rica 'formally withdrew and proclaimed itself sovereign' in 1838

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's row begins in 1840 but the infobox dates the withdrawal from the Federal Republic to 14 November 1838. The shape is unchanged; only the years are extended back.

55,945 km2 against the infobox's 51,180 km2 (ratio 1.09; the shape's bbox reaches Panama at the Sixaola and Burica ends, which is the cell grid's edge, not a claim). The Partido of Nicoya was incorporated by the town-hall vote of 25 July 1824 (77 percent in favour; Santa Cruz three days later; the town of Guanacaste alone declined) and the shape's west edge at 85.89 W takes in the Nicoya peninsula and Guanacaste. Unverified: page budget - the page says 'Until 1849, when it became part of Panama, Chiriquí was part of Costa Rica'; Cliopatria's shape (south edge 8.32 N) has no Chiriquí, no other page opened supports the sentence, and the Coto War page has Coto in Panama's Chiriquí in 1921. The shape stands; a gap-filler should open 'Chiriquí Province'.

56,087 km2, +142 km2 (0.25 percent) on the 1840 shape and back to 55,945 in 2000: no page opened explains either change, and the start of Cliopatria's Panama row in 1905 is the likely trigger. The Coto War page has the Coto hamlet in Panama's Chiriquí until 1921 and Panama made to renounce it; that zone is smaller than the shape's resolution, so the shape is kept and the 1921 gain is flagged in the ledger.

55,945 km2, the 1840 outline again; the infobox gives 51,180 km2 (ratio 1.09). The Costa Rica page has no border change in 2000; the 2009 ICJ ruling and the 2010 Isla Calero dispute are about navigation, not a transfer of land.
Same shape as 2000-2023; infobox area 51,180 km2.

region.text: Costa Rica, including the Nicoya Partido, withdrawn from the Federal Republic of Central America

ledger.note: 1838: Costa Rica withdraws from the Federal Republic of Central America. 'In 1838 ... formally withdrew and proclaimed itself sovereign'; infobox 'from the Federal Republic of Central America: 14 November 1838' (the federation's dossier gives 15 November). The same page says Costa Rica 'formally declared independence in 1847'.

region.text: Virgin Bay and the Transit Route country on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, taken by Costa Rican forces under Mora on 7 April 1856

ledger.note: 1856: Costa Rica takes the war to Nicaragua. Costa Rica declared war on Walker's government on 27 February 1856, the filibusters were beaten at Santa Rosa on 20 March, and Costa Rican forces under Mora captured Virgin Bay on 7 April 1856. The page does not say how long Costa Rican troops stayed or what they held after April, so the whole Rivas department is the researcher's reading of the zone.

region.text: Virgin Bay and the Transit Route country on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, taken by Costa Rican forces under Mora on 7 April 1856

ledger.note: 1857: Walker surrenders and the Filibuster War ends. on 1 May 1857 Walker surrendered to US Navy commander Charles Henry Davis; Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras had formed the Allied Central American Army with the Nicaraguan Legitimists.

ledger.note: 1921: the Coto War begins. The war was 'fought between 21 February and 5 March 1921'; Costa Rican forces under Héctor Zúñiga Mora occupied Pueblo Nuevo de Coto, which Panama retook without combat on 27 February.

ledger.note: 1921: the United States stops the Coto War. On 4-5 March USS Pennsylvania and USS Sacramento arrived and the two countries announced a cessation of hostilities.

region.text: the Coto region, a hamlet on the Coto River in the Alanje district of Chiriquí Province (Pueblo Nuevo de Coto), drawn as a radius around Golfito because the gazetteer lacks the place

ledger.note: 1921: Coto passes to Costa Rica. under US pressure Panama renounced Coto, which passed to Costa Rica (infobox: Pueblo Nuevo de Coto annexed to Costa Rica), enforcing the White Award of 12 September 1914; the border was definitively resolved by a treaty of 1941. The zone is already inside Cliopatria's 1905 shape, so the map shows no change. The Coto War page gives no date for Panama's renunciation or the handover: March is the month the fighting stopped, not a dated transfer (reviewer am-08-f).

wars.name: Filibuster War

zones.text: Virgin Bay and the Transit Route country on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, taken by Costa Rican forces under Mora on 7 April 1856

wars.outcome: Costa Rica declared war on 27 February 1856, won at Santa Rosa on 20 March and took Virgin Bay on 7 April; Walker, inaugurated Nicaraguan president on 12 July 1856, surrendered on 1 May 1857.
wars.note: Guatemala (about 500 men, May 1856), El Salvador (700, June 1856) and Honduras (200, December 1856) joined Costa Rica and the Nicaraguan Legitimists; the page describes no Costa Rican operation on the San Juan River.

wars.name: Coto War

zones.text: the Coto region, a hamlet on the Coto River in the Alanje district of Chiriquí Province (Pueblo Nuevo de Coto), drawn as a radius around Golfito because the gazetteer lacks the place

wars.outcome: 21 February-5 March 1921: Costa Rica occupied Coto and lost it in a Panamanian counter-attack (27 February); United States pressure ended the fighting and Panama renounced Coto to Costa Rica; infobox 'Panamanian territorial victory, Costa Rican legal victory'.
wars.note: The page names the awards: Loubet on 11 September 1900 (rejected by Costa Rica) and White on 12 September 1914 (favoured Costa Rica). The 1941 treaty is the Echandi-Fernández treaty on the border page and the Arias-Calderón treaty on this page.

wars.name: Cañas-Jerez border settlement and San Juan River dispute

zones.text: the right bank of the San Juan River: the treaty 'puts the border on the right bank of the river, giving the river to Nicaragua', with commercial navigation rights for Costa Rica

wars.outcome: The treaty enacted on 15 April 1858 fixed the border from the southern edge of Lake Nicaragua east along the San Juan River; President Cleveland recognised its validity on 22 March 1888; the ICJ upheld Costa Rica's commercial navigation rights on 14 July 2009; a dispute around Isla Calero followed in 2010.
wars.note: No land changed hands on the pages opened; the page does not say the treaty ceded or confirmed Nicoya. The 2009 and 2010 items are from the Costa Rica page.

wars.name: Costa Rican Civil War
belligerents: rebel forces (the page opened names no leader)
wars.outcome: A 'brief civil war in 1948' of 44 days; Costa Rica 'abolished its military force' on 1 December 1948; the current constitution was adopted on 7 November 1949.

certainty.note: The northern frontier was unsettled until the Cañas-Jerez Treaty of 1858 and the Panama frontier was undefined since colonial times (Coto War page).

The Nicaraguan frontier is sharp from the 1858 treaty and the 1888 Cleveland Award (right bank of the San Juan River); the Panamanian frontier stays soft: Loubet award 1900, White award 1914, Coto War 1921.
'The border in its present state is demarcated by the Echandi-Fernandez Treaty of 1941' (Costa Rica-Panama border page); the mouth of the San Juan (Isla Calero) is disputed in 2010.

notes: All five pages of the budget are used. Cliopatria's four shapes are one outline (55,945 km2, +142 km2 in 1905-1999) and no page opened explains the 1905 and 2000 steps. Unsettled: (1) the Costa Rica page's sentence that Chiriquí 'was part of Costa Rica' until 1849 is not reflected in the shape and not supported by the border pages (gap: open 'Chiriquí Province'); (2) the Atlantic-side land Costa Rica earlier ceded to Panama (Coto War page, undated); (3) the 1900 Loubet and 1914 White awards' lines; (4) the 1941 treaty is named Echandi-Fernández on one page and Arias-Calderón on the other; (5) any Costa Rican operation on the San Juan River in 1856-57 (not on the page) and the 1824 Nicoya annexation (before the dossier's start; the page gives the votes of 3 March, 4 July and 25 July 1824 but no year of final incorporation) are not ledger events. Start 1838/11 is the infobox's; the body also says 1847. The seed lists republic-of-baja-california as Costa Rica's neighbour in 1856, when Cliopatria's Nicaragua row has a gap (probably Walker's regime drawn under that Name); the Nicaragua dossier handles 1856. Gazetteer names needed: 'Coto' (the Coto region near Ciudad Neily, Costa Rica-Panama frontier; a Golfito radius is used), 'Virgin Bay' (La Virgen, Rivas, Nicaragua; Rivas department used).
